metadata.title: Type III Error Detector — Wrong Problem, Right Solution
metadata.topic: BEHIND THE MODEL · TYPE III ERROR (WRONG PROBLEM)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: an answer that technically satisfies the problem as stated can still be solving the wrong problem — the fix is stating the problem several honest ways and testing candidate answers against each framing. Lands the carry-out that a right answer to the wrong problem is still wrong.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B06 (the support-ticket ask: hide-the-button answer planted collapsing every framing, returns split by a fourth framing into a search fix that survives some framings and fails others)

beats.narration_text: Someone asks: did Claude get the answer wrong? But check the wrong thing and even a correct answer misses. The real question: did Claude get the problem wrong?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Did Claude get the answer wrong?', hesitates on 'answer', corrects to 'problem'

props.text:
Did Claude
get the answer
wrong?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. Single-word trigger ('answer') swapped for a single-word replacement ('problem') so buildActs()'s whitespace-token match fires cleanly. TIMING LAW: narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('answer' -> 'problem') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Ask Claude to cut support ticket volume, and one answer comes back fast: hide the contact button. Tickets drop from three hundred a week to under fifty. Technically, the ask is satisfied. That's a Type III error — a term from statistician Howard Raiffa — solving the wrong problem, correctly.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a ticket counter falling, a hand hiding a contact button

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the ask satisfied, the button hidden
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A counter reading '300/week' ticking down to 'under 50' while a contact button on a small mock page fades out beneath a hand icon. A label 'ASK SATISFIED' checks itself off beside the counter. THIS EXACT SETUP RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: The natural check is simple: does this satisfy what I asked for? Hide the button, and the ticket count says yes.

shot.new_visual_element: A single checkmark stamped on the ask, no other question raised

production_viz.label: The natural guess - does it satisfy the ask?
production_viz.mechanic: A single problem-statement card ('cut support ticket volume') with one arrow pointing to a lone green checkmark. Nothing else on screen — the point is that only one question got asked.

beats.narration_text: But ask the same problem a second way — why do people need support in the first place — and hiding the button answers nothing. It only stops the counting. One check isn't enough. The fix: state the problem more than one honest way, and see which answers survive all of them.

shot.new_visual_element: The checkmark struck through against a second framing; the problem statement splitting into two

production_viz.label: The break - a second honest framing, no answer
production_viz.mechanic: The B02 checkmark reappears, now struck through in terracotta, beside a second framing card reading 'WHY DO PEOPLE NEED SUPPORT AT ALL?' with a bare question mark where an answer should be. The single problem card from B02 visibly splits into two framing cards.

beats.narration_text: State the problem several distinct ways — zoom out to the bigger goal, zoom in to specifics, swap who's acting — and write one candidate answer for each. Then test every answer against every framing. An answer that only survives its own framing taught you something real. An answer that survives all of them usually means the framings never actually differed.

shot.new_visual_element: Three framings in a row, each with its own answer; arrows testing each answer against the other two

production_viz.label: The mechanism - test every answer against every framing
production_viz.mechanic: Three framing cards in a row — ZOOM OUT, ZOOM IN, CHANGE ACTOR — each with its own candidate-answer card beneath it. Thin arrows fan out from each answer to the other two framings, some landing on a check, some on an X, showing the cross-test.

beats.narration_text: Answers that diverge across framings don't prove you found the right problem — they only prove the framings were genuinely different questions. Which one to act on is still your call.

shot.new_visual_element: Divergent answers, each marked different question, no verdict stamped

production_viz.label: Direction A - divergence isn't proof of the right problem
production_viz.mechanic: The three answers from B04 sit apart, each labeled 'DIFFERENT QUESTION' beneath it, with an arrow pointing up to a blank space where a verdict would go — deliberately empty, no stamp.

beats.narration_text: And answers that collapse into one don't mean nothing else exists — it means keep reframing. Add why is self-service blocked, and a different fix appears: better search. It survives some framings and fails others. That's the signal the button-hiding fix never gave.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the hidden-button answer collapsing all three framings; a fourth framing added; the search fix surviving some, failing others

production_viz.label: The anchor returns - a fourth framing breaks the collapse
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 HIDE-THE-BUTTON ANSWER REAPPEARS, now shown checking all three framings at once (collapsed). A fourth framing card, 'WHAT'S BLOCKING SELF-SERVICE?', slides in; a new answer, 'IMPROVE SEARCH', appears beside it with a mixed check/X pattern against the four framings — the signal the button fix never produced.

beats.narration_text: Getting the right answer to the wrong problem is still getting it wrong. Reframe the problem before you trust the answer.

props.quote: Getting the right answer to the wrong problem is still getting it wrong. Reframe the problem before you trust the answer.
props.sparkLine: Right answer, wrong problem, still wrong.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I want to use Claude as a Type III error detector — checking whether an answer solves the right problem, not just whether it satisfies the problem as stated. Take a task I describe and generate three different honest framings of it. For each framing, write a candidate answer, then test that answer against the other framings. Tell me which answers survive only their own framing, which collapse into all of them, and what that says about whether I'm solving the right problem. Liam, in for Bear.
